title: The Coat Gets Invited

full_text:
A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched work clothes and mud-spattered boots.

The snobbish servants glanced at his rags and pushed him to the drafty corner near the kitchen door. The host walked past him without a word of greeting, and the waiters served him only cold broth and burnt crusts.

Nasruddin quietly slipped away, hurried home, and washed thoroughly. He put on his most magnificent holiday robe—a flowing kaftan of shimmering scarlet silk embroidered with gold thread and trimmed with luxurious fox fur—and donned a grand turban adorned with a silver brooch.

When he returned to the banquet hall, the servants bowed to the floor, opening the double doors with fanfare. The host rushed forward with open arms, embraced the Mulla, and seated him at the head of the banquet table upon velvet cushions.

Waiters immediately brought platters of roasted partridge, saffron pilaf, roasted almonds, and sweet pistachio halva.

Nasruddin smiled graciously. He picked up a spoonful of rich saffron stew and poured it directly into the sleeve of his silk robe! Then he dipped the fur hem of his kaftan into the almond sauce and rubbed sweet halva over his gold embroidery, murmuring affectionately: "Eat, my fine coat, eat! Enjoy the soup! Feast upon the pilaf!"

The host and guests were flabbergasted: "Mulla, what on earth are you doing? Why are you feeding your clothes?"

Nasruddin wiped his hands calmly and replied: "When I arrived an hour ago in my honest human body, wearing my working clothes, you turned me away into the cold corner. But when this coat arrived, you offered velvet cushions and royal delicacies! Therefore, it is obvious that this feast was prepared not for me, but for my coat! And it is only fair that the coat should enjoy what it has earned!"

The host blushed crimson with shame and apologized profusely, while the guests learned a lifelong lesson about the true worth of character over appearances.
moral: People who judge a man by his fine garments are entertaining clothes, not character.
